newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian leaders in Aboriginal land claim summit.
newsitem.headline: Australian leaders in Aboriginal land claim summit.

text.p: Australian leaders will hold an emergency summit on Monday in a bid to end a national row over conflicting land claims by farmers and Aborigines that has damaged business and split political allies.

Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Monday that a speedy and fair solution was important to reduce uncertainty in Australia's valuable agricultural and mining industries, worth billions of dollars a year in exports.
Prime Minister John Howard has summoned state and territory leaders to the capital on Monday to try to end the stalemate in negotiations over competing land claims.
Howard is seeking backing for his 10-point compromise deal, which he says gives Aborigines continued access to land while providing security to farmers and miners.
The key elements of the compromise include confirming farmers' rights over their properties, but guaranteeing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.
Howard has said 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) could be claimed by Aborigines under native title land laws.
The plan has been criticised by Aborigines, farmers and Fischer's National Party, the junior member in Howard's ruling Liberal-National coalition.
As Howard seeks a nationally agreed compromise, consulting Aboriginal and farm groups as well as the states, Fischer said the states could end up legislating their own solution.

Asked if states, which are responsible for land issues, could decide on their own to meet farmers' demands and legislate to abolish Aboriginal rights to land under pastoral lease, Fischer said: "That is an option.
"...the states hold the land bank, the states hold the legislative settings as sovereign state parliaments under our constitution," he said.
But he said he hoped a compromise could be struck that would stop short of the total extinguishing of Aboriginal land rights.

The National Party and farm groups want the abolition of Aborigines' rights to government land let to farmers on long-term leases, but not the extinguishing of Aboriginal rights to land still held by the government.

Miners and farmers have complained that uncertainty has crippled Australia's valuable primary industries since the High Court in December unexpectedly ruled that Aborigines had rights to government land leased to farmers.
